pathway.title: Century Communities, Inc. — Credit Snapshot
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: 1. Leverage has risen sharply on both a weaker earnings base and higher debt. Century Communities, Inc. reported total debt of USD 1,812.587 million at 30 September 2026 against last-twelve-month adjusted EBITDA of USD 294.366 million, or 6.16x, and net debt of 5.87x, up from 2.53x and 2.27x in FY2024 (total leverage has more than doubled in under two years) and 4.13x and 3.81x in FY2025 [CP-1, Documentary Fact for inputs, Analyst Interpretation for the derived ratios]. Holding adjusted EBITDA at its FY2025 level, September 2026 debt alone gives 5.18x, so debt growth and earnings decline each contribute. On unadjusted EBITDA the ratios are 7.68x total and 7.31x net, because adjusted EBITDA adds back inventory impairment, which has occurred in every period shown. Implication: debt service capacity depends on a recovery in volume and margin rather than on deleveraging.

2. Operating cash flow is negative and bank debt funds the gap. Net cash used in operating activities was USD 267.475 million in nine months 2026 against USD 57.654 million a year earlier, inventories rose by USD 382.865 million to USD 3,744.023 million, and the revolver balance rose from USD 51.5 million to USD 456.0 million (net drawings of USD 404.5 million) while still paying USD 27.519 million of dividends and USD 71.198 million of repurchases [CP-1; CP-1A, Documentary Fact]. Mechanic: homebuilding converts cash late, so growth in land and homes under construction absorbs liquidity ahead of closings. Implication: leverage on the company's own homebuilding measure rose to 34.9% net debt to net capital from 25.9%, and a slower sales pace would extend the cash outflow.

3. Liquidity is adequate on reported figures, with a long bond runway. Undrawn revolver capacity was USD 744.0 million after the 30 September 2026 amendment raised commitments to USD 1.2 billion, and company-reported liquidity was USD 863.8 million including cash held in escrow [CP-1]. The first bond matures in August 2029 (USD 500.0 million), the next in September 2033 (USD 500.0 million), and USD 1.1 billion of revolver commitments run to November 2030. The near-term maturities are secured warehouse lines of USD 191.266 million through May 2027 and construction loans of USD 129.450 million from December 2026. Implication: refinancing risk for bondholders is back-ended, but revolver availability depends on covenants that are not supplied.

4. Demand and margin are under pressure from incentives and rates. Third-quarter 2026 average selling price was USD 345.0 thousand against USD 384.2 thousand (down 10.2%), gross margin on home sales was 15.0% against 17.9%, deliveries were 2,442 against 2,486, and the company attributes the price decline to increased incentives and the volume decline to slower absorption, as management's explanation [CP-1A, Management Language]. Selling, general and administrative expense rose to 14.1% of home sales revenue from 12.6% on a partly fixed cost base. Mechanic: price cuts fall straight to earnings, and a large part of the customer base is entry-level buyers, whose demand is sensitive to affordability and mortgage rates [CP-1A, Documentary Fact]. Implication: the earnings base that supports leverage could fall further if rates rise.

5. Interest cover has weakened, with only annual cash interest available. Adjusted EBITDA covered cash interest paid 7.40x in FY2024 and 4.30x in FY2025; for the last twelve months only an accrual proxy of 3.62x exists, because cash interest for 2026 is not disclosed [CP-1, Analyst Interpretation]. Most interest is capitalized to inventory and recognized through cost of sales, so EBITDA is stated before most interest cost. Implication: coverage is declining, and the recent trend cannot be confirmed on a cash basis.

6. The HistoryMaker Homes acquisition adds a cash call outside the reported balance sheet. The company bought the business on 7 October 2026 for initial cash consideration of about USD 160.2 million, adding 29 Texas communities, and the filing does not state how it is funded [CP-1A, Documentary Fact; the Dallas community and delivery targets are Management Language]. Implication: reported September leverage and liquidity understate the position after the deal, and the revolver is the likely but unconfirmed source.

7. Governance is aligned but capital returns continued as borrowing rose. The Executive Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, who are brothers, held 13.9% of shares at 31 December 2025; no related-party leakage, dividend recapitalisation or creditor-adverse transaction is documented, and the company says repurchases use cash and the revolver [CP-1A, Documentary Fact]. Implication: the behaviour reads as Neutral or Mixed, with discretion to cut returns still unused.

cells.text: Development, design, construction, marketing and sale of single-family attached and detached homes in 16 states; in many projects the company also entitles and develops the underlying land. Over 45 markets.
Land development raises capital intensity and inventory exposure; value is realized only at closing.

Century Communities brand serves entry-level, first and second time move-up and lifestyle buyers with limited personalization; Century Complete targets entry-level buyers, sells through retail studios, centralized locations and the internet, and offers no option or upgrade selections.
Entry-level concentration makes demand sensitive to affordability and mortgage rates.
Five reportable homebuilding segments (West, Mountain, Texas, Southeast, Century Complete), plus Financial Services, Century Living and a non-operating Corporate segment.
Diversified regional exposure; each region is a separate operating segment.

Total revenues 2,581.367 (US$m): West 493.990, Mountain 538.799, Texas 417.153, Southeast 416.327, Century Complete 646.107, Financial Services 68.991. Shares 19.1%, 20.9%, 16.2%, 16.1%, 25.0% and 2.7%.
Analyst Interpretation (shares derived from printed amounts)
Century Complete is the largest segment and is a low-price, no-option model; no region exceeds a quarter of revenue.
Home sales revenues 2,474.127 of total revenues 2,581.367 in nine months 2026, which is 95.8%; land sales and other 38.249; Financial Services revenues 68.991.
Earnings are driven by closings; land sales are small and lumpy, so revenue visibility rests on backlog.

New homes delivered 2,442 against 2,486; average sales price of new homes delivered 345.0 thousand against 384.2 thousand; net new home contracts 2,284 against 2,386. Nine months: 6,961 against 7,357 deliveries, average price 355.4 thousand against 382.7 thousand, contracts 7,278 against 7,624.
Lower price and volume reduce operating leverage on a partly fixed cost base.

Deliveries decreased 1.8% and 5.4%, primarily due to slower absorption rates from lower demand; average price decreased 10.2% and 7.1%, primarily due to increased use of incentives. Mortgage rates rose further in Q3 2026; adjustable-rate mortgages were nearly 35% of mortgages originated by principal in Q3 2026, against less than 5% in Q1 2025.
Incentives and rate buydowns transfer margin to buyers and raise cancellation and refinancing risk if rates rise after closing.
Backlog 1,106 homes with value 413,956 (US$ thousands) at 2026-09-30 against 1,117 homes and 416,924; selling communities at period end 343 against 321.
Backlog of about one quarter of deliveries gives limited forward visibility; more communities add capacity but also inventory.

Homebuilding gross margin 15.0% in Q3 2026 against 17.9%, including impairment of 19,605 (US$ thousands); selling, general and administrative expense 14.1% of home sales revenue against 12.6%, which the company attributes to decreased revenue on a partially fixed cost base.
Documentary Fact; attribution is Management Language
Operating leverage works against the company when volume and price fall.

60,969 lots owned and controlled at 2026-09-30, of which 33,473 owned and 27,496 controlled, against 60,916 at 2025-12-31; land bought for cash through bulk purchases or option contracts, with obligations under options generally limited to forfeiting deposits of 84.6 (US$m, 77.5 non-refundable).
Option-heavy control (45.1% of lots, derived) lowers owned-land risk but the company still expects to perform on the majority of contracts within 24 months.
Construction takes three to four months; about 96% of homes delivered in the first nine months of 2026 were priced below FHA-insured mortgage limits and about 98% were built as move-in-ready homes.
Short cycle and spec inventory shorten the cash cycle but expose the company to carrying finished homes in a weak market.
Inventories 3,744,023 against 3,361,158 at 2025-12-31 (US$ thousands); net cash used in operating activities 267,475 in nine months 2026; purchases of property and equipment 21,647.
Inventory build consumes cash ahead of closings; capital spending is small, so cash flow is driven by working capital.
Home starts, construction costs and cash outflows are historically highest in the second and third quarters; most cash receipts from deliveries occur in the second half.
Cash needs peak in the second and third quarters, so a year-end balance sheet may not show the intra-year trough in liquidity.

Inspire Home Loans Inc. originates mortgages for the company's homebuyers and generally sells loans within 30 days, financing them through repurchase facilities; loans held for sale at fair value 186.5 (US$m); net gains on sale of loans 13.1 in Q3 2026; segment income before tax 6.2 in Q3 2026.
A captive lender supports sales but adds a funding line that is non-guaranteed by the parent and exposes the company to loan repurchase and rate-lock risk.

Multi-family rental development in Colorado, reported separately from Q1 2025; strategy since Q1 2025 is predominantly to dispose of properties shortly after lease stabilization; multi-family rental properties inventory 241.704 (US$m) at 2026-09-30; one 300-unit property was sold in 2025.
Non-core, construction-loan-funded asset class whose exit timing and pricing are not disclosed.
Section 45L tax credits are disallowed for homes delivered after June 30, 2026 under H.R.1; the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act became law in July 2026, with an uncertain impact.
A loss of tax credit benefit raises the effective tax rate on 2026 second-half deliveries.

runs.text: Strengths. (1) Liquidity and maturity profile [Documentary Fact; CP-1]: USD 744.0 million undrawn on the revolver, USD 86.086 million of cash, no bond before August 2029, so near-term refinancing is limited to bank and warehouse lines. (2) Diversified operations [Documentary Fact; CP-1A]: five regional homebuilding segments across 16 states, none above 25.0% of nine-month revenue, with Century Complete the largest, which limits single-market exposure. (3) Flexibility of land and cash use [Documentary Fact; CP-1A]: about 45.1% of lots are controlled through options with obligations generally limited to deposits, and dividends and repurchases are discretionary. (4) Insider alignment [Documentary Fact; CP-1A]: 13.9% ownership by the two senior executives. (5) Equity cushion [Documentary Fact; CP-1]: stockholders' equity of USD 2,560.998 million against total debt of USD 1,812.587 million.

Weaknesses. (1) High and rising leverage [Analyst Interpretation; CP-1]: 6.16x adjusted EBITDA and 7.68x unadjusted. (2) Negative operating cash flow [Documentary Fact; CP-1]: bank-funded growth and returns. (3) Margin compression [Documentary Fact; CP-1A]: price cuts via incentives on a partly fixed cost base. (4) Floating-rate bank dependence [Documentary Fact; CP-1]: the revolver of USD 456.0 million, repurchase facilities and construction loans carry floating rates, and the revolver's covenants are not visible. (5) Acquisition and capital allocation [Documentary Fact; CP-1A]: a USD 160.2 million cash purchase while the company continued buybacks, with funding unstated. (6) Structural subordination [Documentary Fact; CP-1]: unsecured notes sit behind at least USD 320.716 million of identified secured debt and the non-guarantor mortgage subsidiary's lines.

runs.text: The transaction of record after the balance sheet date is the acquisition, completed on October 7, 2026, of substantially all of the assets and certain liabilities of HMH Lifestyles, L.P., doing business as HistoryMaker Homes, a Dallas-area homebuilder, for initial cash consideration of approximately $160.2 million, subject to customary holdbacks and post-closing adjustments (Q3 10-Q page:7, page:34). It adds 29 active communities to the Texas segment (Q3 10-Q page:7). The company says it will increase its Dallas division's active communities from 12 to 41 as of September 30, 2026 and triple trailing-twelve-month deliveries from 211 to 669 homes, and its outlook includes 100 deliveries from the acquired business in the fourth quarter (Q3 release page:1, page:3); these are Management Language, not filed fact. The company also states it will keep a land relationship with HistoryMaker's sister land development company (Q3 release page:2). Because the deal closed after September 30, 2026, the acquired assets and assumed liabilities are not in the balance sheet, purchase accounting is incomplete, and the filing does not state how the cash consideration is funded. This is a subsequent event and it is kept out of every September 30, 2026 figure. Parties other than the target, any sponsor, a use-of-proceeds statement, and the effect on liquidity are Not supplied; the missing funding statement matters because revolver borrowings already stood at $456.0 million and nine-month operating cash flow was negative (financial base handoff).

New debt and financing events are as follows. On September 30, 2026 the company signed the First Amendment to its Credit Agreement dated November 1, 2024 (administrative agent U.S. Bank National Association): commitments rose from $1.0 billion to $1.2 billion, maturity for participating extending lenders moved to November 1, 2030 with $100.0 million still maturing November 1, 2028, new lenders were added, certain financial covenants were revised, and the 0.10% credit spread adjustment was eliminated (Q3 10-Q page:16). The revised covenant terms are not supplied. In September 2025 the company issued $500.0 million of 6.625% senior notes due September 2033 and extinguished $500.0 million of 6.750% senior notes due 2027 at 100% of principal, for $511.4 million including accrued interest, with a loss on extinguishment of $1.4 million (10-K page:75). Earlier, the revolver was raised from $900.0 million to $1.0 billion on April 22, 2025 (10-K page:77). No new bond issue after September 2025 appears in the sources. The mortgage repurchase facilities, construction loans and revolver are described in the financial base handoff.

fields.value: Century Communities, Inc. is a US single-family homebuilder that operates in 16 states and over 45 markets under two brands, Century Communities and Century Complete, with a captive mortgage, title, insurance and escrow business and a small multi-family rental development segment in Colorado. Revenue is almost wholly home sales, which depend on affordability, mortgage rates and the use of incentives; the company itself ties its latest price decline to incentives and its lower deliveries to slower absorption. The transaction that matters most to a creditor is the October 7, 2026 purchase of the assets of HistoryMaker Homes in Dallas for about $160.2 million of initial cash, which is a post-balance-sheet event that adds communities and deliveries but also a cash call whose funding is not stated, coming days after the September 30, 2026 revolver amendment that raised commitments to $1.2 billion. Ownership is public with no sponsor; the Executive Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, who are brothers, hold a documented 13.9% stake and have employment agreements with change-of-control severance. No dividend recapitalisation, related-party leakage or creditor-adverse transaction is documented in the sources, but the proxy material and debt agreements that would show control rights, baskets and permitted payments are not supplied, so legal capacity is not assessed. The facts that move the credit most are demand and margin resilience, funding of the acquisition and shareholder returns while operating cash flow is negative, and the structural subordination of the unsecured notes to secured construction and warehouse debt.

fields.value: The transaction of record after the balance sheet date is the acquisition, completed on October 7, 2026, of substantially all of the assets and certain liabilities of HMH Lifestyles, L.P., doing business as HistoryMaker Homes, a Dallas-area homebuilder, for initial cash consideration of approximately $160.2 million, subject to customary holdbacks and post-closing adjustments (Q3 10-Q page:7, page:34). It adds 29 active communities to the Texas segment (Q3 10-Q page:7). The company says it will increase its Dallas division's active communities from 12 to 41 as of September 30, 2026 and triple trailing-twelve-month deliveries from 211 to 669 homes, and its outlook includes 100 deliveries from the acquired business in the fourth quarter (Q3 release page:1, page:3); these are Management Language, not filed fact. The company also states it will keep a land relationship with HistoryMaker's sister land development company (Q3 release page:2). Because the deal closed after September 30, 2026, the acquired assets and assumed liabilities are not in the balance sheet, purchase accounting is incomplete, and the filing does not state how the cash consideration is funded. This is a subsequent event and it is kept out of every September 30, 2026 figure. fields.value: Century Communities, Inc. has a weakened but still liquid credit profile in which earnings are falling faster than debt is being repaid. The strongest support is USD 744.0 million of undrawn revolver and USD 86.086 million of cash at 30 September 2026, no bond maturity before August 2029, and a 16-state footprint with a captive mortgage arm [CP-1; CP-1A]. The weakest point is leverage: total debt reached 6.16x last-twelve-month adjusted EBITDA, from 2.53x in FY2024, while nine-month operating cash flow was negative USD 267.475 million and revolver borrowings funded inventory, buybacks and dividends. The outcome will be decided by covenant headroom, which the sources do not show, by how the USD 160.2 million HistoryMaker Homes purchase is funded, and by whether incentive-driven margin pressure eases.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 1. Leverage has risen sharply on both a weaker earnings base and higher debt. Century Communities, Inc. reported total debt of USD 1,812.587 million at 30 September 2026 against last-twelve-month adjusted EBITDA of USD 294.366 million, or 6.16x, and net debt of 5.87x, up from 2.53x and 2.27x in FY2024 (total leverage has more than doubled in under two years) and 4.13x and 3.81x in FY2025 [CP-1, Documentary Fact for inputs, Analyst Interpretation for the derived ratios]. Holding adjusted EBITDA at its FY2025 level, September 2026 debt alone gives 5.18x, so debt growth and earnings decline each contribute. On unadjusted EBITDA the ratios are 7.68x total and 7.31x net, because adjusted EBITDA adds back inventory impairment, which has occurred in every period shown. Implication: debt service capacity depends on a recovery in volume and margin rather than on deleveraging.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 2. Operating cash flow is negative and bank debt funds the gap. Net cash used in operating activities was USD 267.475 million in nine months 2026 against USD 57.654 million a year earlier, inventories rose by USD 382.865 million to USD 3,744.023 million, and the revolver balance rose from USD 51.5 million to USD 456.0 million (net drawings of USD 404.5 million) while still paying USD 27.519 million of dividends and USD 71.198 million of repurchases [CP-1; CP-1A, Documentary Fact]. Mechanic: homebuilding converts cash late, so growth in land and homes under construction absorbs liquidity ahead of closings. Implication: leverage on the company's own homebuilding measure rose to 34.9% net debt to net capital from 25.9%, and a slower sales pace would extend the cash outflow.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 3. Liquidity is adequate on reported figures, with a long bond runway. Undrawn revolver capacity was USD 744.0 million after the 30 September 2026 amendment raised commitments to USD 1.2 billion, and company-reported liquidity was USD 863.8 million including cash held in escrow [CP-1]. The first bond matures in August 2029 (USD 500.0 million), the next in September 2033 (USD 500.0 million), and USD 1.1 billion of revolver commitments run to November 2030. The near-term maturities are secured warehouse lines of USD 191.266 million through May 2027 and construction loans of USD 129.450 million from December 2026. Implication: refinancing risk for bondholders is back-ended, but revolver availability depends on covenants that are not supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 4. Demand and margin are under pressure from incentives and rates. Third-quarter 2026 average selling price was USD 345.0 thousand against USD 384.2 thousand (down 10.2%), gross margin on home sales was 15.0% against 17.9%, deliveries were 2,442 against 2,486, and the company attributes the price decline to increased incentives and the volume decline to slower absorption, as management's explanation [CP-1A, Management Language]. Selling, general and administrative expense rose to 14.1% of home sales revenue from 12.6% on a partly fixed cost base. Mechanic: price cuts fall straight to earnings, and a large part of the customer base is entry-level buyers, whose demand is sensitive to affordability and mortgage rates [CP-1A, Documentary Fact]. Implication: the earnings base that supports leverage could fall further if rates rise.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 5. Interest cover has weakened, with only annual cash interest available. Adjusted EBITDA covered cash interest paid 7.40x in FY2024 and 4.30x in FY2025; for the last twelve months only an accrual proxy of 3.62x exists, because cash interest for 2026 is not disclosed [CP-1, Analyst Interpretation]. Most interest is capitalized to inventory and recognized through cost of sales, so EBITDA is stated before most interest cost. Implication: coverage is declining, and the recent trend cannot be confirmed on a cash basis.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 6. The HistoryMaker Homes acquisition adds a cash call outside the reported balance sheet. The company bought the business on 7 October 2026 for initial cash consideration of about USD 160.2 million, adding 29 Texas communities, and the filing does not state how it is funded [CP-1A, Documentary Fact; the Dallas community and delivery targets are Management Language]. Implication: reported September leverage and liquidity understate the position after the deal, and the revolver is the likely but unconfirmed source.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 7. Governance is aligned but capital returns continued as borrowing rose. The Executive Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, who are brothers, held 13.9% of shares at 31 December 2025; no related-party leakage, dividend recapitalisation or creditor-adverse transaction is documented, and the company says repurchases use cash and the revolver [CP-1A, Documentary Fact]. Implication: the behaviour reads as Neutral or Mixed, with discretion to cut returns still unused.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths. (1) Liquidity and maturity profile [Documentary Fact; CP-1]: USD 744.0 million undrawn on the revolver, USD 86.086 million of cash, no bond before August 2029, so near-term refinancing is limited to bank and warehouse lines. (2) Diversified operations [Documentary Fact; CP-1A]: five regional homebuilding segments across 16 states, none above 25.0% of nine-month revenue, with Century Complete the largest, which limits single-market exposure. (3) Flexibility of land and cash use [Documentary Fact; CP-1A]: about 45.1% of lots are controlled through options with obligations generally limited to deposits, and dividends and repurchases are discretionary. (4) Insider alignment [Documentary Fact; CP-1A]: 13.9% ownership by the two senior executives. (5) Equity cushion [Documentary Fact; CP-1]: stockholders' equity of USD 2,560.998 million against total debt of USD 1,812.587 million.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Weaknesses. (1) High and rising leverage [Analyst Interpretation; CP-1]: 6.16x adjusted EBITDA and 7.68x unadjusted. (2) Negative operating cash flow [Documentary Fact; CP-1]: bank-funded growth and returns. (3) Margin compression [Documentary Fact; CP-1A]: price cuts via incentives on a partly fixed cost base. (4) Floating-rate bank dependence [Documentary Fact; CP-1]: the revolver of USD 456.0 million, repurchase facilities and construction loans carry floating rates, and the revolver's covenants are not visible. (5) Acquisition and capital allocation [Documentary Fact; CP-1A]: a USD 160.2 million cash purchase while the company continued buybacks, with funding unstated. (6) Structural subordination [Documentary Fact; CP-1]: unsecured notes sit behind at least USD 320.716 million of identified secured debt and the non-guarantor mortgage subsidiary's lines.
